children: said Wednesday that its Legion infrared sensor system successfully exchanged targeting information between two F-16 fighter jets during flight tests in Arizona, demonstrating a potential way to track airborne threats without relying on radar.

The tests were conducted with the Air National Guard and Air Force Reserve Test Center. Two F-16s departing from Morris Air National Guard Base in Tucson carried Legion pods equipped with a pre-production version of L3Harris Technologies’
The data link connected the two sensor pods in flight, allowing them to combine information and improve the accuracy of their target tracks, according to Lockheed Martin

Legion, previously known as IRST21, is an infrared search-and-track system that passively detects the heat signatures of aircraft. Unlike radar, it does not transmit signals that could reveal the location of the aircraft carrying it.

Connecting two pods also allows the system to establish the range to multiple targets more quickly. That capability could help pilots distinguish among contacts, reduce workload and shorten the time needed to develop an engagement plan in contested airspace.

said Legion’s open architecture allows the system to incorporate communications equipment and other capabilities. The company is flight testing the networked system on F-16s under an Air National Guard contract to evaluate its performance, portability and compatibility with other platforms.
Future development could include software-defined radios, gateways supporting multiple communications waveforms and links between crewed and uncrewed aircraft.

The demonstration supports Lockheed’s effort to expand Legion from a stand-alone infrared sensor into a networked targeting system that could attract additional integration and upgrade work. Because Legion is already in production and fielded on U.S. Air Force aircraft, a successful data-link upgrade may offer a lower-risk growth opportunity than an entirely new weapons program. disclosed no contract value, production commitment or expected revenue from the capability, while HiveLink remains in a pre-production configuration.
Wider use is the longer-term opportunity
Legion is available in a podded configuration for F-15 and F-16 aircraft. Lockheed Martin said the system also could be moved to other fighters, support aircraft and unmanned platforms.

L3Harris designed HiveLink to provide line-of-sight and beyond-line-of-sight communications in contested environments. The system uses mesh networking and is intended for platforms with tight limits on size, weight and power.

said its earlier infrared search-and-track systems have accumulated more than 300,000 flight hours on F-14 and F-15 aircraft. The latest test indicates that the company is seeking to build on that installed base by enabling aircraft to share passive sensor data, particularly during missions in which radar use is limited or undesirable.
